newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian jobless rate to stay high.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian jobless rate to stay high.

text.p: Australia's February labour force report is expected to add to the growing pile of evidence that the economy has moved past its slowest point and is well positioned for stronger growth in 1997.
Thursday's data is expected to show a fifth successive rise in jobs, evidence of the economy's gathering strength.

"Our view remains that employment growth will continue to gather pace over the course of 1997 and 1998 in line with a pickup in economic growth more generally," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist David Bassanese said in a report.

But while the number of jobs has been growing, unemployment remains stubbornly fixed around 8.5 percent and further substantial improvement may now require structural reform of the labour market, economists said.

The median forecast of the 29 economists Reuters surveyed was for a February jobs rise of 10,000 after January's downwardly revised rise of 28,400. Forecasts range from a fall of 10,000 to a rise of 18,000.

Some felt that the strong December quarter meant the risks to forecasts was to the downside, especially given that gains had been dominated by part-time jobs which might have been only for over the Christmas and New Year period.
The median forecast would mean that employment levels would have risen by just over 79,000 in the last five months.
"Job creation will be an important issue for 1997," GIO Australia chief economist Akis Haralabopouls said.
"Markets and policy makers will be looking to see the fruits of the expected growth/low inflation mix in stronger employment growth and a gradual reduction in the unemployment rate.
However, despite this recent strength in jobs the unemployment rate was seen as being barely affected.
Unemployment rate forecasts centre on 8.6 percent, with the 8.3 to 8.8 percent range of forecasts also the parameters of the band that has contained the unemployment rate over the last 13 months.
Confusing the forecasting process somewhat were revisions to the labour force data announced last week.
These lowered the total number of people employed by around 15,000, but left the general trend of strengthening employment through the last quarter of the year intact.
The unemployment rate was unchanged at 8.6 percent.

The revisions were due to the annual reanalysis of seasonal adjustment factors and were not related to the lower employment estimates that have occured since the introduction of a new telephone survey method.

But regardless of the understatement of jobs growth caused by the new survey method and the expectations of stronger growth through this year, economists said the outlook was for unemployment to remain at around 8.0 percent or higher for much of 1997 given current labour market policies.

Three interest rate cuts and the cyclical improvement in the economy could only do so much, economists said, and the structure of the labour market needed to be freed for unemployment to make a sustainable downward move.
Macquarie Bank chief economist Bill Shields said that the cyclical upswing in the economy should see jobs growth in 1997.

"The key issue in my judgement is structural, however. There is no doubt we need greater flexibility in Australia in the labour market, most particularly in relative and aggregate wage settings," he said.
"And I think without that, we will not see unemployment fall much below 8.0 percent, despite the strength of the recovery we might get in the next year or two," Shields said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
